content_of_post_to_comment: I’m a single mother. And I mean single all the way: care, maintenance, education, the whole thing. I homeschool my daughter. I work full time. I have no weekends , and lately there are very few empty spaces anywhere else. Today I ate standing in the kitchen. At some point I realized I was simultaneously preparing tomorrow’s class for my daughter, working on the branding for my own work, and writing an essay with my AI. I was tired as hell but I was also smiling. Because somewhere inside that chaos, I was making something that lights me up. There is a conversation about AI-generated writing that reduces it to slop. And certainly, slop exists. But that is not what happens when we write. We take our time. We argue. We research. We find papers. I bring messy thoughts that sometimes exist only as a feeling that there is something here, and together we pull at them until I can see what I actually think. We discard things. Rewrite things. Push ideas until they either hold or collapse. AI makes possible for someone with almost no spare time to say what she already had inside her. That’s the part I wish we talked about more. My voice gets to leave the kitchen. My ideas get to become essays. Things that might have remained half-formed in my head while I prepared classes, answered emails, made chocolate milk and kept a household moving can become something another person gets to read. And tonight, tired as hell, I find that extraordinarily beautiful.
comment: The interesting shift here is that AI is not just accelerating output; it is changing who gets to participate in intellectual life. The unresolved question may be how we preserve the human struggle behind ideas while removing the barriers that kept many voices invisible.
